name: Vinpocetine

card.summary: Semi-synthetic periwinkle derivative sold in Europe as a prescription drug and in the US as a supplement; evidence for benefit in dementia or stroke is described as unsupported by full reviews, and the FDA warns about pregnancy.
card.note: FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development; US regulators consider it an unapproved new drug.

quick.overview:
Vinpocetine is a synthetic derivative of vincamine, an alkaloid from the lesser periwinkle. It was developed in Hungary and sold there as Cavinton, and has been used for decades in parts of Europe and Asia for cerebrovascular disorders. In the US it is sold as a "nootropic" supplement.

Wikipedia says the evidence does not fully support a benefit in either dementia or stroke. There are no studies of vinpocetine for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proposed actions include sodium channel blockade, reduced calcium influx, antioxidant activity, PDE1 inhibition and inhibition of IKK, which affects NF-kappaB inflammatory signalling.
quick.risks: Reported effects include flushing, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn and blood-pressure changes. The FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development. US regulators regard it as an unapproved new drug and a 2015 analysis found many supplement labels inaccurate.

lead: Vinpocetine (ethyl apovincaminate) is a synthetic derivative of the vinca alkaloid vincamine, which is extracted from lesser periwinkle (Vinca minor) leaves or Voacanga africana seeds.[1] Grokipedia (AI-generated) describes it as developed by the Hungarian company Gedeon Richter and marketed in Hungary as Cavinton from 1978.[2]

People who take it do so as a nootropic: the aim is sharper focus, memory and mental stamina for studying, work and training, with cerebral blood flow and neuroprotection as the stated mechanisms. A systematic review of cognitive enhancers among university students lists vinpocetine among the non-prescription substances students use as study aids.[17] This is the wiki's "focus and cognition" route to better performance rather than a direct change to appearance.

It has been used for more than three decades in several Asian and European countries for cerebrovascular disorders, although Wikipedia states that the evidence does not fully support a benefit in dementia or stroke.[1] In the United States it is sold as a supplement even though the FDA regards it as an unapproved new drug.[1]

Appearance is not the stated use of vinpocetine; it enters the wiki's looks-adjacent territory through the nootropic route, where focus, study stamina and training mindset are the goals. No published study has tested it for appearance outcomes.

paras: Prescribed for cerebrovascular disorders such as stroke and dementia in various countries.[1] Registered trials have also looked at epilepsy[3], Parkinsonian disease[4], diabetic nephropathy[5] and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.[6]

Vinpocetine lacks one hydroxyl group relative to vincamine and is the ethyl ester rather than the methyl ester, with formula C22H26N2O2.[1] Grokipedia says Gedeon Richter chemists patented the synthesis in 1973 and that it was introduced in Hungary as Cavinton in 1978.[2]
Cochrane reviews on vinpocetine appeared for acute ischaemic stroke in 2000 and 2008, and Wikipedia mentions a 2003 review for cognitive impairment and dementia.[13][14][1]

Vincamine, the parent alkaloid, is found in the leaves of lesser periwinkle and can also be semi-synthesised from related alkaloids such as tabersonine; it is sold as a prescription medicine for dementia in parts of Europe and has itself been studied as a nootropic.[19] The lesser periwinkle has a long folk-medicine use in Europe, but the structured literature on vinpocetine begins with the Hungarian development programme and its clinical studies in the 1970s to 1990s.[2][20]

Postulated mechanisms include sodium channel blockade, reduced calcium influx and antioxidant activity; PDE1 inhibition and IKK inhibition have been reported in laboratory studies.[1] A 2010 paper reported that vinpocetine inhibits NF-kappaB-dependent inflammation through an IKK-dependent but PDE-independent mechanism.[7] Its poor oral bioavailability has prompted formulation research with lipid nanoparticles.[8][9]

Wikipedia gives oral bioavailability of about 56.6 percent and an elimination half-life of about 2.5 hours, with hepatic metabolism and renal excretion.[1] Lab studies it cites report PDE1 inhibition in isolated rabbit aorta (1984), IKK inhibition that blocks NF-kappaB translocation (2010) and increased DOPAC in rat striatal nerve endings (2001).[1]

The 2000 Cochrane review of vinpocetine for acute ischaemic stroke found one trial in 40 patients, with data for 33: no deaths, no significant difference in dependency versus placebo and no adverse effects reported; the reviewers concluded that there was not enough evidence to evaluate survival or dependency.[13] The 2008 update included two trials with 70 participants.[14]

Wikipedia notes that as of 2003 three controlled trials had tested vinpocetine in older adults with memory problems, and that a 2021 phase II open-label study examined sensorineural hearing loss.[1][16] A 2021 study in Epilepsy & Behavior examined whether vinpocetine could enhance cognition in healthy volunteers and patients with epilepsy and compared blood levels of the drug and its active metabolite in humans and animals.[15] A 1987 randomised trial examined vinpocetine against cognitive impairments produced by flunitrazepam.[18]

Registered studies include a trial of NF-kappaB-dependent inflammation in acute ischemic stroke patients, a 610-person Chinese assessment in cerebral infarction, a trial of a multi-ingredient nootropic in healthy young volunteers and studies in epilepsy, Parkinsonian disease and diabetic nephropathy; registry entries describe design, not results.[3][4][5][10][11][12]

The Cochrane review of vinpocetine for cognitive impairment and dementia, first published in January 2003, included three randomised trials with 583 people with dementia, all from around the early 1990s or earlier. The authors reported that improvements over placebo were tentative, few patients were treated for six months or more, adverse effects were few at the doses studied, and larger trials in well-defined groups were needed.[20]

Flushing, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn and transient blood pressure changes are reported.[1] In 2019 the FDA warned that vinpocetine may cause a miscarriage or harm fetal development.[1]

In September 2016, according to Wikipedia, the FDA concluded vinpocetine is ineligible as a dietary ingredient because of its synthetic nature and proposed therapeutic uses, making it an unapproved new drug in the US; in the EU it is prescription-only. It remains widely sold as a supplement, often marketed as a nootropic.[1]

A 2015 analysis of 23 brands sold at US supplement retailers found only 6 gave accurate dosages and 6 contained no vinpocetine despite listing it; 17 of 23 gave no quantity information, and a US senator asked the FDA to suspend sales and asked ten retailers to stop selling the products.[1] On 3 June 2019 the FDA warned women of childbearing age about pregnancy risks from supplements containing vinpocetine.[1]

The Procera AVH brand, which combined undisclosed amounts of vinpocetine with huperzine A and acetyl-L-carnitine, was the subject of a 2012 class-action settlement of $500,000 and a 2015 FTC ruling that its memory and cognitive-decline claims were false, misleading and unsubstantiated; the defendants agreed to pay $1.4 million and to a permanent injunction against similar claims.[1] Its founder was charged with deceptive expert endorsements.[1]

Reporting on the June 2019 FDA advisory said the warning rested on animal findings of reduced fetal weight and increased miscarriage risk, that the agency advised women who are or could become pregnant to avoid vinpocetine supplements, and that it asked sellers to review labels for pregnancy warnings.[21] Wikipedia's vincamine article notes that in the US vinpocetine-class products may be sold as supplements labelled for adult use of six months or less, and that the National Toxicology Program has recorded concerns about long-term use.[19]

Vinpocetine ('Vinpo') appears in T Nation nootropic and supplement threads from about 2007 to 2011 as a component of memory and focus stacks, alongside DMAE, aniracetam, oxiracetam and caffeine.[22] Members' reports in a 2009 study-aid thread were mixed: some said it was fine for long-term use in such stacks and that effects took weeks of regular use, while others reported no noticeable effect, harder concentration or mental cloudiness.[22]
The discussion is about cognition and training focus rather than appearance, and these reports are anecdotes rather than trial results.

lore.intro: On T Nation and nootropic forums vinpocetine is discussed as a memory and focus supplement, typically in stacks, with mixed personal reports.[22]

claims.believers: Forum members stack it with DMAE and racetams and describe stronger effects when combined, with benefits building over weeks.[22]
claims.experts: The Cochrane dementia review found only tentative improvements in older trials and called for larger studies; a 2021 study examined cognition in healthy volunteers and people with epilepsy.[15][20]

claims.believers: Nootropic users cite improved blood flow to the brain as the mechanism.[22]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists postulated mechanisms including sodium channel blockade, reduced calcium influx, antioxidant activity and PDE1 inhibition, largely from laboratory studies.[1]

claims.claim: It is safe for long-term supplement use.
claims.believers: One 2009 poster called it fine for long-term use in a stack.[22]
claims.experts: The FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or fetal harm based on animal data, and a 2015 analysis found many supplement labels inaccurate.[1][21]

claims.claim: Supplement labels reliably contain what they say.
claims.believers: Products are sold as nootropics with listed amounts.[1]
claims.experts: A 2015 analysis of 23 brands found only 6 with accurate dosages and 6 with no vinpocetine at all.[1]
A 2010 laboratory paper reported NF-kappaB-dependent inflammation inhibition via an IKK-dependent mechanism, and a registered trial studies this in stroke patients.[7][10]

angle.text: People take vinpocetine as a nootropic for focus and memory. It is not used on the face or body, so any link to looks runs through study, work and training performance.
